Protecting Yourself from Air Pollution and Toxins So aside from exercising outdoors whenever possible and taking the steps above to protect yourself during exercise, what can you do to minimize the effects of air pollution? Here are my top eight suggestions.
1. BREATHE THROUGH YOUR NOSE WHENEVER
POSSIBLE. The air we breathe isfirst processed through the nose, which is lined with tiny hairs called cilia thatfilter, humidify, and warm or cool the air before it enters the lungs.
It is estimated that these cilia protect us from over twenty billion particles of foreign matter every day. And there are many other benefits to nasal breathing.
For example, breathing in and out through the nose helps you take fuller, deeper breaths, which stimulates the lower lungs to distribute greater amounts of oxygen throughout the body.

The lower lungs are rich with the parasympathetic nerve receptors associated with calming the body and mind, whereas the upper lungs, which are used in chest and mouth breathing, are associated with hyperventilation and trigger sympathetic nerve receptors, which are involved infight-or-flight reactions.

Here’s another benefit: the lungs actually extract oxygen from the air during both exhalation and inhalation, and because the nostrils are smaller than the mouth, air exhaled through the nose creates a backflow of oxygenated air into the lungs.
Plus, because we tend to exhale more slowly through the nose than we do through the mouth, the lungs have more time to extract oxygen from the air we’ve already taken in.
Proper nose breathing also reduces hypertension and stress and keeps you from overexerting yourself during a workout.
Finally, your sinuses produce nitric oxide, which, when carried into the body through the breath, can open blood vessels and combat harmful bacteria and viruses.

During the COVID pandemic, both Anders Olsson and Patrick McKeown wrote about the potential benefits of nasal breathing against viral infections, highlighting how many people never consider the nose’s unexpected role in triggering a cascade of hormones and chemicals that lower blood pressure and ease digestion.
Immune function, weight, circulation, mood, and sexual function can all be heavily influenced by the Amount of nitric oxide in the body.

In fact, the popular erectile dysfunction drug sildenafil (aka Viagra) works by releasing nitric oxide into the bloodstream, which opens the capillaries in the genitals and elsewhere, and nasal breathing does the same thing.

Studies looking at the relationship between nitric oxide and SARS (a form of coronavirus) showed that nitric oxide has a potent effect helping to neutralize the virus and inhibiting replication. Who knew nasal breathing could be so powerful?

6. USE NATURAL HOUSEHOLD CLEANERS. From toilet bowl cleaners to laundry detergent, synthetic, chemical-based cleaners are an enormous source of health issues and environmental pollution.
For example: • Tide laundry detergent has high levels of 1,4-Dioxane, a carcinogenic contaminant.
(In people who are sensitive to molds and mycotoxins, Tide is a major trigger for chemical sensitivity reactions.)
• Most fabric softeners contain synthetic fragrances that can cause respiratory irritation, headaches, and autoimmune reactions.
• All-purpose cleaners contain the sudsing agents diethanolamine (DEA) and triethanolamine (TEA).
When these substances come into contact with nitrites in the environment or your body and mouth, they react to form nitrosamines carcinogens.
In contrast, if you peek into the cleaning cabinet of the Greenfield home, you’ll see three basic ingredients: lemons, baking soda, and white vinegar.
These three ingredients form the basis of our household cleaning solutions, from disinfectants to window cleaners.

Sure, occasionally we’ll throw in essential oils such as tea tree, oregano, thieves (a blend of cloves, lemon, cinnamon, eucalyptus, and rosemary—I talked about it at length in chapter 15), or lemon, but even then, you’llfind no strange chemicals.
Fact is, there are many inexpensive, easy-to-use natural alternatives that can safely be used in place of commercial household products.
You’ll find a list of the best natural household cleaning ingredients and recipes for cleaning solutions on here to here, along with plenty of additional helpful recipes on BoundlessBook.com/20.

chunks.content: 7. CHOOSE THE RIGHT FURNISHINGS. Your new carpet or cabinet could be slowly poisoning you with chemicals such as benzene, ethylene glycol, or formaldehyde via a process called off- gassing.

In one test of furniture for a baby’s nursery, a rocker put offseven times more formaldehyde than the state of California considers safe, the paint for the nursery containedfive times the amount of chemical gases as the recommended limit, and more than one hundred chemicals wafted from the crib mattress, including alcohols and industrial solvents.
The good news is that many furniture items emit low or no levels of hazardous chemicals, especially those with a Greenguard certification.
Stem Furniture is one company that produces furniture with absolutely zero VOCs.
When it comes to engineered wood, such asflooring or cabinets, look for an indoor air quality low-emission certification, such as one from Greenguard or SCS Global Services.
In addition, look for non- VOC paint, and as an alternative to vinylflooring, consider natural linoleum.
8. BE COGNIZANT OF MOLD AND MYCOTOXINS. Mycotoxins, as you may recall from chapter 4, are toxic compounds produced by various species of mold.

Among a variety of other health issues, they can cause mitochondrial dysfunction, asthma and other breathing issues, cancer, cardiovascular disease, altered kidney and liver function, disrupted sleep, stunted muscle recovery, miscarriage, and a bad case of fuzzy brain.

There are a host of mycotoxins and molds in foods That are commonly perceived to be healthy, and the website SurvivingMold.com is a good tool for discovering whether a food you frequently eat may be tainted with dead organic matter that is deleteriously affecting your health and performance.

In a nutshell, unless you completely trust the source or the amount of time it’s been around, I’d seriously reconsider the blue cheese at the salad bar and other potentially moldy foods, including sour cream, buttermilk, and sour milk; cured, pickled, and smoked meats andfish; prepackaged meats, like lunch meats, salami, smokedfish, and some sardines; commercial, store-bought pickles, olives, capers, salad dressing, or ketchup; vinegar and soy sauce; and the average hotel room coffee.

I’m not saying you have to live your life completely abstaining from these foods, but you should go out of your way to avoid them if you don’t know how they were packaged or how long they have been open to the environment. But mycotoxins aren’t just found in food.

By getting a test such as an ERMI (environmental relative moldiness index) from a licensed contractor (I don’t recommend this as a DIY project), you mayfind that your house has toxic mold that produces bacteria that can often be more deadly than what youfind in food.

When an area of moisture forms in your house, within twenty-four to forty-eight hours mold can form, chomp down, and multiply on just about any part of your home that mold considers a food source, including dust, wood, paint, paper, cotton, oil, and modern building materials like drywall.

To avoid mold formation and exposure, I recommend you do the following: • Keep house dust to a minimum. Mop allfloors and dust all surfaces at least once a week. Use a vacuum cleaner with a HEPAfilter.
HEPA- filter vacuums capture the widest range of particles and potential allergens.
• Use a dehumidifier in mold-prone rooms such as basement bathrooms.
• Use an oscillating fan in the bathroom after showering andfix any leaks as soon as possible.
• Regularly clean surfaces where mold usually grows—around showers and tubs and beneath sinks.
• Be conscious of toxins in carpeting, especially in products made from synthetic materials. Buy natural-fiber wool and cotton rugs.

If you really want to take things to the next level, replace your wall-to-wall carpeting with hardwoodfloors, all-natural linoleum, or ceramic tiles, and use nontoxic glues, adhesives, stains, or sealers for installation.

• Seal or replace particle board walls,floors, and cabinets, which often contain formaldehyde, which emits unhealthy fumes. Avoid any synthetic, strong-smelling plywood,fiberglass,fiberboard, and paneling.
• Consider adding a WaterCop around every drain, sink, and bathtub in your home.
This device will shut offthe water to the house at thefirst sign of a leak. Most models are wireless, but there are wired options, too.
The Best Natural Household Cleaners
The natural cleaning ingredients below can all be used alone or combined to create nontoxic cleaning solutions for many applications.

At right are recipes for some of my favorites, and you can find many more thorough instructions for anything you’d ever need at Eartheasy.com, which is an organic living website owned by my friend Aran Seaman.
Of course, if you don’t have time, you don’t have to make your own cleaning supplies.

There are a growing number of commercial nontoxic home- cleaning products, and you can find these and other organic, natural products, from kitty litter to diapers, on websites such as EWG.org, ThriveMarket.com, and OrganicConsumers.org.

On BoundlessBook.com/20, you’ll find links to some of the products I recommend most. Baking sodacleans and deodorizes. Rubbing alcoholis good for cleaning floors, especially tile. Borax, despite its scary name, is simply sodium borate.
It cleans, deodorizes, disinfects, softens water, and cleans wallpaper, painted walls, and floors. It is also good for killing mold.

[[IMG id=image-1248-270 index=21 alt="Image from page 1248"]] [[IMG id=image-1248-271 index=22 alt="Image from page 1248"]] [[IMG id=image-1248-272 index=23 alt="Image from page 1248"]] [[IMG id=image-1248-273 index=24 alt="Image from page 1248"]] If you want to know if you have been exposed to mold, there are a few options.
In the US, you can get mold exposure tests that you’ll learn about momentarily, or you can simply pay attention to symptoms.

If you suddenly begin to experience allergy-like symptoms such as asthma, congestion, frequent sickness, headaches, joint pain, or brain fog, and you’ve recently moved into a new house or apartment or haven’t changed anything in your diet, you should suspect mold.
Chapter 4 explained how to get tested for mold exposure and some exercises you can do if you have been exposed.
I also recommend revisiting chapter 13 and following the detoxification instructions there.

Finally, if the laundry list of potentially mold-containing foods above makes you nervous or stressed about your diet, I recommend you do a simple Coca pulse test after you eat a meal that is a frequent staple in your diet and you suspect may be causing symptoms.
This basically involves using a phone app (I use one called NatureBeat) and a connected chest strap heart rate monitor to track your heart rate before, during, and after eating.
If your heart rate increases byfive or more beats after eating, you may have an allergy to the food, or there may be mycotoxins in it.
In plain terms, the change in your heart rate indicates that your body is going into fight-or-flight mode after eating—which is not a good sign! Need more resources?

Three good books for discovering how to de- mold your house areMy House Is Killing Me!andThe Mold Survival Guide, both by Jeffrey C. May, andThe Mold Medicby Michael Rubino (Rubino also has a great list of resources for mold prevention, remediation, and more at Homecleanse.com/mold-resources).
You should also check out my podcast with “The Moldfinder” Brian Karr, which I’ll link to on the resources page for this chapter.
WATER
In my hometown of Spokane, Washington, they don’tfluoridate the water, and boy, am I glad. Fluoride is certainly a crucial compound—in pesticides, that is.
That’s right: sodiumfluoride is a registered insecticide and rodenticide that is used in rat and roach poisons.
It is a toxic waste by-product of the manufacturing of phosphate fertilizers and the aluminum-refining industry, which means it also has a lot of lead as well as other toxic substances in it.
But it’s cheaper to simply dumpfluoride into our water supply than to pay toxic waste disposal fees.
Unfortunately, this can cause cancer, hip fracture, dentalfluorosis, stained teeth, neurological impairment, lower IQ in children, and learning disorders.

Sure,fluoride certainly has a good antidecay effect when you apply it directly to the tooth itself—but you don’t have to swallow the stuff, and frankly, when it comes to tooth decay, there is little to no difference between countries withfluoridated water and countries with nonfluoridated water.

If you really want to dig into the issue withfluoride, listen to a podcast that I recorded with Paul Connett, coauthor of the eye- opening bookThe Case Against Fluoride(the podcast is linked to on BoundlessBook.com/20), or read the bookThe Fluoride Deceptionby Christopher Bryson.
Of course,fluoride isn’t the only issue with water.
Since 2004, testing by water utilities has consistently found thousands of pollutants in the tap water we drink on a daily basis.
More than half of the chemicals detected are not subject to health or safety regulations and can legally be present in any amount.

Unfortunately, at least in the US, the federal government has not set a single new drinking-water standard since 2012—and water utilities spend nineteen times more on water-treatment chemicals every year than the federal government invests in protecting lakes and rivers from water pollution in thefirst place.
Chlorine is probably one of the more common chemicals that many health enthusiasts encounter in the gym or in drinking water.

Particularly in swimming pools that are not naturally cleaned, we soak up chlorine through our skin while simultaneously breathing in chloramines, the toxic by-products that form when chlorine reacts with organic matter such as dead skin cells.

If you’re a swimmer, a triathlete, or someone who hits the pool or hot tub often, you’re likely getting exposed to plenty more chlorine than you’re drinking in your municipal water supply or from a glass of tap water at a restaurant.

And even if you’re not a swimmer, you’re still getting significant skin exposure to chlorine simply from showering or bathing in your city’s water (if you’re not using thefiltration methods I’ll describe shortly).
This chlorine exposure can cause both cell wall damage and internal soft tissue damage, along with autoimmune, asthma, and allergy issues.
If you’re notfiltering your water, chlorine can even vaporize from toilet bowls and into the air as you wash your clothes or dishes!
But perhaps you’re already aware that chemicals in water are an issue.

Perhaps you’re also aware of the importance of drinking enough water, and that your body consists mostly of water, which is needed for just about every physiological process and biochemical reaction that exists, including blood circulation, metabolism, body temperature regulation, and detoxification.

But did you know there are different types of water that go far beyond regular H O?2 EZ Water and DDW In his TEDx Talk “Water, Cells, and Life” and his booksThe Fourth Phase of WaterandCells, Gels, and the Engines of Life, University of Washington professor Gerald Pollack explained the role of water in the functioning of Cells and the importance of negatively charged structured water, also known as exclusion zone (EZ) water.
This water can both hold and deliver electrical energy, much like a battery.

Typical tap water is simply H O, but 2EZ water is actually H O , which is more viscous and alkaline than regular 3 2water and has a refractive index about 10 percent higher, allowing it to more readily respond to light photons from sources such as an infrared sauna, photobiomodulation light panels, and sunlight.
It is also the same kind of negatively charged water that your cells and extracellular tissue naturally contain.
This is important because cell membranes are hydrophilic (water-loving) surfaces with a net negative charge, and EZ water can accumulate next to these hydrophilic surfaces.
As negatively charged particles from the water and the cell membranes repel each other, energy is created.
This is because a key factor that allows positive charges to migrate into a cell is the water surrounding the cell.

The electrical conductivity of water acts like a battery that drives the cellular machinery by inducing a charge separation that is able to shuttle positive protons along the cellular cytoskeleton while leaving negatively charged electrons in the water.

If you always thought this was achieved by a sodium-potassium pump, as most biology textbooks still teach, then you should look up the work of Gilbert Ling on PubMed, where you’llfind research articles that thoroughly debunk the notion of a sodium- potassium pump.

Dr. Thomas Cowan wrote in his booksHuman Heart, Cosmic Heartand Cancer and the New Biology of Waterabout how this negative charge allows blood, which consists largely of water, to more easily navigate through the chambers of the heart, reducing cardiovascular strain and increasing overall heart health.

In addition, my former podcast guest Dr. Stephanie Seneffhas an excellent TEDx Talk about how negatively charged ions in EZ water help to generate sulfate, which enhances cellfluidity and reduces any tendency for cells to clump, particularly when sunlight is present.

EZ Water may even upregulate p53, a transcription factor that acts as a potent tumor suppressor and modulator of DNA damage, making it potentially useful for cancer therapy. Then there’s deuterium-depleted water (DDW).
DDW—which can be purchased in bottles or created by a DDW generator—is also known as “light water” and contains a very low concentration of deuterium.
Deuterium is a hydrogen isotope that has roughly double the mass of a hydrogen atom.

This means that high amounts of deuterium in the body— which are often found in people who have been exposed to pesticides, herbicides, municipal water, a high-sugar or acidic diet, or many other unhealthy scenarios—can displace hydrogen and deleteriously impact cell function. Reducing levels of deuterium can restore proper cell function and health.

I strongly suspect that hydrogen-enriched water (which I talked about in chapter 12), structured water, and DDW are three forms of water that are going to receive plenty of attention in the wellness world over the next decade as people come to realize that not all water is created equal.

How to Manage Exposure to Metals I spend time in my basement infrared sauna at least three times a week, because saunas have been shown to be an excellent way to release metals through the skin, and because I know that everything from brake dust on the road to metals in airports and airplanes to the occasional sushi binge exposes me to my fair share of metals.

If it’s not cleaned up and removed from the body, this type of chronic metal exposure can cause chronic fatigue, poor mood, disrupted sleep, headaches, poor immune system function, low hormone levels, and brain fog. The biggest culprit for metal exposure is modern dentistry.

Even though about 50 percent of dentists in the US are now mercury-free, only an estimated 10 percent of dentists fully understand the health risks associated With amalgam fillings—which contain toxic mercury, despite what the term silver filling might lead you to believe.

If you decide you want to pull the metal out of your mouth, then you should know that the process of removing and replacing amalgam fillings comes with the risk of acute toxicity from the mercury released during the removal process, and this can cause serious damage to organs such as your liver and kidney.
Because of this, and because other metals can get absorbed into your mouth when you’re at the dentist, my family and I only go to a holistic dentist (also known as a “biological dentist”).
These dentists make a special effort to limit your exposure to toxins and chemicals.

When they’re removing amalgam fillings, they use a cold-water spray to minimize mercury vapors, put a dental dam in your mouth so you don’t swallow or inhale any toxins, use a high-volume evacuator near the tooth at all times to evacuate the mercury vapor, wash out your mouth immediately after the fillings have been removed, and use powerful air purifiers in each room.
They also take precautions during regular cleanings, such as using natural products to ensure you are not exposed to chemicals and toxins.

One option for finding a good dentist is to call my dentist (introduced in chapter 17)—Dr. Eniko Loud at Whole Health Dentistry in Phoenix, Arizona— to inquire about becoming her patient or get a recommendation for someone near you who uses her same techniques, but the following organizations can also help you find a holistic dentist: • Consumers for Dental Choice • International Academy of Biological Dentistry & Medicine (IABDM) • Dental Amalgam Mercury Solutions (DAMS) • Huggins Applied Healing • Holistic Dental Association
• International Association of Mercury Safe Dentists Unfortunately, you can get heavy-metal exposure from all sorts of sources that go way beyond metal in your mouth.
These sources include: • Smog • Car keys • Toys made in China • Secondhand cigarette smoke • Pesticides and herbicides • Protein powders and dietary supplements
• “Pristine” water (like my local Lake Coeur d’Alene) that in fact has high amounts of mining runoff • Food stored in metal containers • Big fish like tuna and dolphin

• Nuclear fallout from the Fukushima disaster in Japan You can get tested for heavy metals via an HTMA test or any of the toxin tests you can find at the BenGreenfieldLife.com recommended tests page, but if you’ve been exposed to any of the above, you can assume you’d benefit from pulling metals out of your body.
Binding heavy metals and pulling them out of your body is called chelation, and many substances can do this.
The metals generally exit your body in stool, urine, hair, breath, and sweat.
Some forms of chelation are accomplished with drugs such as DMPS, but the website DMPSBackfire.com shows you some of the serious problems that can be caused by conventional chelating drugs.
Chelators bind by way of ionic bonds, which are the attractions between the positive charge of a heavy metal and the negative charge of the chelating molecule.
Because of this, chelation can extract precious minerals from your body, but it can also spread metals throughout your body, so that they wind up deposited elsewhere.
So to get heavy metals out of your body, I do not recommend chelation drugs or natural chelation.
Instead, I recommend you use natural compounds that can gently draw heavy metals out of your body.
As with most detoxification programs, you can’t simply pop a supplement or chug a giant bottle of activated charcoal water and walk away.

Instead, to ensure that metals and other toxins are actually removed and don’t travel throughout the body, you need to follow a specific, systematized detox protocol. Review chapter 13 for more information on proper detoxification.

According to Pollack, you can build EZ water naturally in your cells by not only drinking pure and preferably structured water (described later in this chapter), but also by chilling your water, exposing your water to Sunlight or infrared light, drinking fresh vegetable juice, drinking coconut water blended with turmeric, exposing your bare skin to sunlight, using an infrared sauna, and walking barefoot outside, which allows you to absorb negatively charged ions from the surface of the earth.

According to Robert Slovak, whom I interviewed in a podcast (linked to at BoundlessBook.com/20), the same can be said for DDW: instead of purchasing relatively expensive DDW water to add small amounts to your drinking water during the day (a good strategy if you have very high deuterium levels, a problem I discuss in my “Deuterium Demystified” podcast with the Center for Deuterium Depletion in Los Angeles), you can achieve low deuterium levels by lowering your carbohydrate intake and increasing your healthy fat intake, which allows your body, through the process of beta-oxidation, to produce its own DDW!

Who knew water was so much more complex than just H O?2 Best Practices for Pure Water You’re no doubt aware that we live in a modern postindustrial era in which our water isfilled with chemical contaminants from bleach, salts, pesticides, metals, toxins, and drugs, along with biological or microbial contaminants that include bacteria, viruses, protozoans, and parasites, and even radiological contaminants such as cesium, plutonium, and uranium.

So what can you do to ensure you’re protecting yourself from contaminants and chemicals in your drinking water, bathwater, and cooking water, while at the same time consuming water that is in the most natural, ancestral, mitochondria-supporting state possible? Here are my top six tips.
1. FILTER YOUR WATER.
When it comes tofiltering your water, the gold-standard method is to install a whole-house carbon blockfiltration system or reverse osmosis (RO) system.
Carbonfilters are less expensive but effective at removing chlorine and large particulates.
They can also remove 10 to 15 percent of total dissolved solids (TDS).
However, a carbonfilter can’t remove all contaminants as thoroughly as an RO system can.
ROfilters, which work by pushing water through a microscopicfilter material, remove 95 to 97 percent of TDS. They canfilter down to 0.001 micron, which is 500 times smaller than most carbonfilters.
However, they can also remove minerals, so the system should have remineralization technology to add them back in. Demineralized water is also more acidic.

So, to make your water healthy with good minerals once again and to increase its alkalinity, you can remineralize it with trace liquid mineral drops, use sea salt liberally, make Hunza water (structured water rich in hydrogen and minerals that also has a naturally high pH— you canfind instructions for making it on BoundlessBook.com/20), or dress up your drinks and diet with extra electrolytes and minerals.
To transform your RO water into EZ water, you may want to install a whole-house structured water system along with your RO system.

The website GreenfieldWater.com (founded by my father and now operated by my sister) has a variety of both whole-house and portable structured- waterfilters that easily allow you to create your own EZ structured water (the Hunza water mentioned above is also naturally high in EZ water).

For example, one of Greenfield Water’s popular whole-housefiltration systems combines activated carbon with minerals in a highly porous block filter and then structures the water after it has passed through thefiltering system.
This unique carbon adsorbent can soak up a variety of organic and inorganic substances, including chlorine and chloramine, which can be difficult to remove.
It provides the highest-quality drinking water possible from a carbon blockfilter and simultaneously structures the water, which Enhances both absorption and hydration.
Other features include pH adjustment technology and a turbo descaler that reduces scale and is a good alternative to a salt-based water softener.
In my current home, I use the fanciest system on the market: Ophora, which employs a fourteen- stagefiltration process to deliver ultra-purified, oxygen-infused, and mineral-balanced water.
Finally, if you’re serious about drinking water, avoid hot water and tap water whenever you are on an airplane.
Mostflight attendants will not even drink hot water on the plane, including coffee or tea. Why?
The tap water on a plane is delivered to the airport via a water tanker truck where it is stored in a facility.
Then another truck isfilled from the storage tank and delivers the water to the plane.
The water can be contaminated at any point during transport, and indeed has tested positive for pathogenic coliform bacteria, which indicates that human fecal waste is present.
This is not surprising considering that the plane’s water tanks are disinfected only every three months!
So, whenflying—if you don’t want to be drinking “poop”—bring your own water or drink bottled only!
2. USE FILTERS ON ALL FAUCETS. If you forgo a whole-house RO system, then at least purchase a countertop RO system and showerhead and faucetfilters.

In a conversation I had with renowned water expert Robert Slovak, he told me about a reverse osmosis purifier that presents none of the bacteria issues of a standard tank-based RO system, is incredibly affordable, and can be placed on any countertop.
Called an AquaTru, it uses a miniaturized version of the same reverse osmosis technology used by all the major bottled water brands.

I highly recommend you also install a KDF showerhead and faucet or Fixt showerheadfilter in your bathroom (after all, if you’refiltering the water that goes into your mouth but not the water that comes in through Your skin, it’s a bit of a wasted effort). You’llfind links and discount codes on BoundlessBook.com/20.
3. USE GLASS INSTEAD OF PLASTIC BOTTLES. This is a no-brainer: just don’t use plastic.
If you must travel with a plastic bottle or drink from a plastic bottle while exercising, use a BPA-free brand that alsofilters your water, such as Berkey, LifeStraw, Fixt, or LifeDefender.
This will save you plenty of money on bottled water, especially while traveling through airports.

I also recommend stainless- steel bottles from a company such as Yeti or, better yet, a MOBOT water bottle, which doubles as a foam roller-esque deep tissue massage device. Consider how many plastics you’re using in your kitchen.
For example, for sous vide cooking, I use Stasher brand bags, which are heat-resistant bags made of food-grade silicone rather than the thin plastic that comes with most sous vide machines.
Instead of a coffee maker that uses plastic fittings and tubes, I opt for a stainless-steel French press.
I also use glass Pyrex containers for storing food rather than Tupperware-style plastic containers.
Finally, don’t get stuck in a hotel with the average hotel plastic bottled water, and definitely don’t pay $8.75 for the glass bottle in the minibar.
Instead, do as I do and preorder through Amazon or Instacart to your hotel, and make yourfirst stop a grocery store where you can grabfiltered water in glass bottles.
See the sidebar for some of my other go-to grocery items when I’m staying at a hotel with a kitchenette or an Airbnb.
4. FIND A LOCAL NATURAL SPRING.
If you want to get as close to a natural source of water as possible, visit FindASpring.com to browse through a user-created database of natural springs around the world.
You’d be surprised at how much free, mineral- rich, clean spring waterflows in an area that’s often just a few minutes From your front door.
Armed with a glass carboy, you can legally and inexpensively harvest it for drinking or bathing!
5. MAKE SURE YOU GET THE RIGHT MINERALS AND
VITAMINS. Sulfate, cholesterols, and minerals are important for adequate water absorption.

Get sufficient amounts of cobalamin (vitamin B ), 12glutathione, iron (preferably from grass-fed animal sources), sulfur (from broccoli, cauliflower, garlic, onions, and liver), zinc (shellfish and black ant extract are good sources), fresh air, grounding or earthing, and sunlight.

Replenish minerals and electrolytes by adding quality salts to food and water and using products like 10X, LMNT, Quinton, Manna Shilajit, or BEAM minerals. Avoid exposure to glyphosate and heavy metals.
For the sulfur piece, it’s a good idea to check your DNA data to see if you’re sulfur sensitive, as it’s a common sensitivity and requires caution with high intake of sulfurous foods.

6. MANAGE CHLORINE EXPOSURE. To mitigate the damages of chlorine, especially on days that you’re in a chlorinated pool or hot tub,fight the oxidation by getting the following into your body: • 2 to 5 g of vitamin C • 2,000 to 4,000 IU of vitamin D • 10 to 20 IU of a natural source of vitamin E that includes tocotrienols, mixed with omega-3 fatty acids (I recommend Designs for Health Annatto-E and Kion Omega) • A diet rich in wild plants, herbs, and spices Unfortunately, most soaps and shampoos that are designed to strip chlorine from skin and hair are laden with endocrine disruptors and dangerous personal-care-product chemicals.

Many people seem to feel just fine when they eat pesticide-laden produce.
This is because you won’t necessarily feel the effects immediately after pesticide exposure.
In fact, the biggest danger from pesticides is the harm that comes from repeated low-dose exposure.
Recent data collected by the EPA reports that in the US alone, approximately five billion pounds of active pesticide ingredients are applied to our foods annually.

That’s a tremendous amount of poison entering our bodies, and, sure enough, a 2002 University of Washington study found that 109 out of 110 urban and suburban children had pesticides in their urine samples, which is even scarier when you consider how prevalent pesticide exposure has become since then.
Food grown on certified-organic farms contains significantly less pesticide residue than food grown with synthetic pesticides.

That may seem obvious, but the evidence for this fact has only been available since 2002, when research proved that children fed organic food have lower residues of certain pesticides in their bodies than children fed conventionally grown food.

So buy certified-organic produce or, if you’re at a farmers market or can contact a company by phone or through their website, ask what type of pesticides or herbicides they do or do not use, since many small manufacturers can’t necessarily afford a certified organic label.
If you really want to make an educated decision and fill your body with the most nourishing and least damaging produce, I recommend you check out the bookRich Food, Poor Food.

And for that simple vinegar trick I mentioned to remove the pesticides and herbicides from nonorganic produce?

Simply mix a solution of½cup vinegar and 5 cups water as a bath in your kitchen sink and then briefly place your Nonorganic vegetables or fruit in the solution, swish them around, and rinse thoroughly in plain water.
But solving the produce problem doesn’t address the entire scenario: you also need to watch out for the pesticides and herbicides in your yard.

After all, the average suburban lawn soaks up ten times as much chemical pesticide per acre than conventional farmland, with over seventy million tons of fertilizers and pesticides applied to residential lawns and gardens annually! I’ll admit, I’m not a huge fan of lawns.

My wife and I prefer to dig up most of the trimmed, neat grass or sod in the yard and replace it with fruit trees and a big, dirty vegetable garden fertilized with compost, which reigns supreme in the world of natural fertilizers.

But if you do want that pristine expanse of green grass, the only way to reduce your dependence on chemical lawn fertilizers is to develop a healthy lawn that is naturally resistant to weeds, insects, and disease, using the following steps:1.
Improve the soil.You can get a lawn pH tester for a few bucks.
When you test, it should read between 6.5 and 7.0, which is slightly acidic.

Soil that is too acidic needs a sprinkling of lime, and soil that is not acidic enough needs a sprinkling of sulfur.2. Choose native grass.Grasses vary in preferred climate, required water and nutrients, shade tolerance, and the degree of wear they can withstand.
Ask your local garden center to recommend grass that is well adapted to your area.3.
Mow often, but don’t trim the grass too short.Giving your lawn a marine cut is not the best idea because surface roots become exposed, the soil dries out faster, and surface aeration is reduced.
Don’t cut off more than one-third of the grass at any one time, and shoot for grass that’s about 2.5 to 3.5 inches high.
When your lawn is finished growing for the season, cut it a bit shorter, to about 2 inches.

This will minimize the risk of mold buildup during the winter.4. Water deeply, but not too often.Regular watering encourages your lawn to develop deep root systems, which make the lawn hardier and more drought-resistant. But be sure you let the lawn dry out before rewatering.
Most healthy lawns require only 1 inch of water per week, which is about fifteen to twenty minutes’ worth of sprinkling once per day.
It’s best to water in the early morning, when less water will be lost to evaporation.
5.Use natural lawn fertilizer.I recommend the Ringer brand, which is a mix of certified-organic minerals.

Consider just a few snippets of the daily routines of a handful of successful pop culture, historical, and political icons, all from the book Daily Rituals: How Artists Work: Secretary of state and president John Quincy Adams skinny-dipped in the Potomac River in the morning, always trying to see how long he could swim without touching the bottom (he got up to 80 minutes before his wife told him to stop).
After putting his kids to bed, President Obama went over briefing papers and did paperwork and then read a book for pleasure for a half hour before turning in.

Stephen King writes every day of the year without exception, beginning work between 8:00 and 8:30 a.m. He has a glass of water or cup of tea and takes a vitamin pill each day, ensuring he is in the same seat and his papers and desk are arranged in the same way every single day.
King has a daily writing quota of two thousand words and rarely allows himself to quit until he’s reached his goal.

Harvard dropout and founder of Facebook, Mark Zuckerberg, is well known for almost always wearing a plain gray T-shirt, saying in a 2014 interview that wearing the same shirt helps allow him to make as few decisions as possible.

These novelists, poets, playwrights, painters, philosophers, scientists, and mathematicians all had daily rituals (often automated and slightly subconscious), such as waking early or staying up late; self-medicating with a morning doughnut or a hot bath; drinking vast quantities of coffee (it is said the philosopher Voltaire consumed forty tofifty cups per day); or taking long daily walks.

Novelist Thomas Wolfe, for instance, wrote standing up in the kitchen, the top of the refrigerator as his desk, dreamily fondling his male configurations (and you thought my infrared-light-on- the-balls trick was strange!).
Philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre ingested ten times the recommended dose of corydrane (a mix of amphetamine and aspirin) each day.
Philosopher René Descartes preferred to linger in bed, his mind wandering in sleep through woods, gardens, and enchanted palaces where he experienced every pleasure imaginable.

British author Anthony Trollope made himself write three thousand words each morning (precisely 250 words everyfifteen minutes for three hours) before going to his job at the postal service, which he kept for thirty-three years, during which time he wrote more than two dozen books.

Choreographer George Balanchine did most of his work while ironing, and composer and pianist George Gershwin worked for twelve hours a day from late morning to midnight, composing at the piano in pajamas, a bathrobe, and slippers.

chunks.content: Beginner The diets in this beginner section are clean eating protocols that aren’t meant to be followed permanently, but instead temporarily implemented for cleansing, detoxification, and preparing for a less restrictive diet after one to twelve weeks.
These are somewhat restrictive plans that I do not necessarily recommend following for life unless you have a serious condition such as celiac or Crohn’s disease or severe food allergies.

If you’ve been eating a diet or living a toxic or unhealthy lifestyle that has caused gut damage, inflammation, sugar dependency, or similar gut problems, I recommend that you follow any of the diets in this section before progressing to an intermediate plan.
If you have more serious gut issues, autoimmune symptoms, or a condition like dysbiosis, stick to this type of diet until your symptoms subside, which sometimes takes up to six months.

(In the case of the GAPS diet, it is recommended that you follow it for up to two years to fully heal a leaky gut.) If you need to detox or cleanse at any point throughout the year, you can return to one of these diets—for example, you can perform a one-to-two-week liver cleanse in the spring and winter or follow an Elemental Diet for thefirst thirty days of each year.

Ultimately, rather than recommending one single diet—which you know from chapter 14 is aflawed approach—I’m equipping you with a number of diets that you can use to heal your gut, ease digestion, detox your body, and prepare your digestive system for more variety.
AUTOIMMUNE PALEO (AIP) DIET
Also known as the Paleo autoimmune protocol, the AIP diet is a much stricter version of the Paleo diet (which is based on meat,fish, vegetables, nuts, and seeds).
It eliminates dairy, grains, eggs, nightshades, legumes, and other foods that may cause inflammation in people with a leaky gut.

As explained in chapter 13, leaky gut can lead to an autoimmune response in which your own immune system tags your tissues, such as your eyes or nervous system, with certain types of antibodies, including those listed below.
This falsely signals to your immune system that those tissues are foreign invaders, and your immune system then attacks those tissues.
Each autoimmune disease also has markers specific to that condition, and BoundlessBook.com/21 includes more information on which antibodies are specific to which diseases.
By focusing on nutrient-rich foods and avoiding inflammatory ones, the AIP diet aims to heal inflammation and any holes in the gut.
People who follow the AIP diet typically should follow it strictly for four to eight weeks and then slowly reintroduce foods that they have been avoiding.
The best book to accompany this diet isThe Autoimmune Paleo Cookbookby Mickey Trescott, since it has a host of tasty recipes that don’t taste like cardboard.

After you’ve spent at least four to eight weeks on one of the diets in this section, the Wahls Protocol (outlined in the intermediate section) is also an excellent diet for managing autoimmunity long term.
You may be a good candidate for the AIP diet if you have elevated antibodies as indicated by an autoimmune blood test, leaky gut syndrome, or a diagnosed autoimmune condition.

Basic symptoms suggestive of autoimmune disease can also include chronic fatigue; joint pain or stiffness; muscle weakness; skin rashes; gastrointestinal symptoms such as bloating, diarrhea, or constipation; and systemic inflammation.

Blood tests may reveal markers of autoimmune activity, such as elevated levels of antibodies directed against specific tissues or organs, like anti-nuclear Antibodies (ANA), anti-thyroid antibodies (e.g., anti-TPO, anti-Tg), anti- citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), or anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (anti-tTG).

Genetic testing may identify specific gene variations associated with autoimmune susceptibility, such as HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 for celiac disease or specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles for autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or type 1 diabetes.

Gut testing, such as comprehensive stool analysis or intestinal permeability testing, may reveal imbalances in gut microbiota, intestinal inflammation, or increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are commonly associated with autoimmune conditions.
Urine testing may assess levels of specific metabolites or inflammatory markers, providing additional insight into immune function and systemic inflammation.

SPECIFIC CARBOHYDRATE DIET (SCD)

The Specific Carbohydrate Diet (SCD) wasfirst described by Sidney V. Haas in 1924 as a way to treat celiac disease and was further refined in the 1951 medical textbookThe Management of Celiac Disease.
It was later repopularized in 1987 by Elaine Gottschall, the mother of one of Haas’s patients.
The SCD is a gluten-free and grain-free diet and was a popular treatment for celiac disease decades before gluten was even discovered.

The diet eliminates complex carbohydrates such as grains, starches, most dairy products, sugars, and processed foods while emphasizing nutrient- dense foods that are easily digested and absorbed, including lean proteins, certain fruits, nonstarchy vegetables, nuts, and healthy fats.

By reducing the intake of fermentable carbohydrates that can fuel pathogenic bacteria and promote inflammation in the gut, the SCD aims to restore balance to the gut microbiota, reduce intestinal inflammation, improve digestive function, and alleviate symptoms.
It may be supplemented with probiotics, digestive enzymes, and other gut-supportive nutrients to further enhance gut healing and optimize digestive health.
I recommend you follow this plan if you have IBD, IBS, bloating, gas, or gut inflammation, particularly if these issues are brought on by gluten or grain consumption.
The best book to accompany the SCD program is Gotschall’sBreaking the Vicious Cycle.

Symptoms of conditions that may benefit from the SCD diet include chronic gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, and/or constipation, as well as systemic symptoms such as fatigue, joint pain, and weight loss.

Blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation, such as elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) or fecal calprotectin, which are commonly associated with inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.
Genetic testing may identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to IBD, such as NOD2/CARD15 mutations.

Gut testing, including comprehensive stool analysis or microbial profiling, may uncover imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, or increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are common features of conditions like IBD, IBS, and other gastrointestinal disorders.
Urine testing may assess levels of specific metabolites or inflammatory markers, providing additional insights into gut health and systemic inflammation.
Based on these assessments, individuals with confirmed or suspected gastrointestinal conditions such as IBD, IBS, or celiac disease and related symptoms may benefit from following the SCD.

GUT AND PSYCHOLOGY SYNDROME (GAPS) DIET

Dr. Natasha Campbell-McBride, a neurologist and nutritionist, developed the GAPS diet and wrote the bookGut and Psychology Syndrometo assist her patients—especially children—who were experiencing problematic gut-brain issues.
Like the SCD, the GAPS diet removes potentially problematic foods, particularly grains and gluten-containing foods, but it also focuses on adding healing, nutrient-dense foods.
If you have cognitive issues, irritation, brain fog, or nervous system–based problems affected by the gut, such as ADHD, this can be a good program to follow.

The diet emphasizes nutrient-dense whole foods that are easily digested and absorbed, while eliminating potentially inflammatory or allergenic foods that may contribute to gut dysbiosis and inflammation.

It typically involves three stages: the Introduction diet, which focuses on healing and sealing the gut lining; the Full GAPS diet, which includes a wider variety of foods while continuing to support gut health; and the Maintenance diet, which is tailored to individual needs and focuses on long-term gut maintenance and overall health.

By removing potentially Harmful foods and incorporating gut-healing foods such as bone broth, fermented foods, and nutrient-dense vegetables, fruits, and healthy fats, the GAPS diet aims to reduce inflammation, support digestive function, and improve neurological and psychological symptoms.
It may be supplemented with probiotics, digestive enzymes, and other gut- supportive nutrients to further enhance gut healing and optimize overall health and well-being.

Symptoms of conditions that may benefit from the GAPS diet include gastrointestinal issues such as chronic bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and constipation, as well as neurological or psychological symptoms such as anxiety, depression, mood swings, and cognitive difficulties.

Blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation or immune dysregulation, such as elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines or antibodies, which are commonly associated with conditions like IBS, IBD, autoimmune disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions.
Genetic testing may identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to gut dysbiosis, inflammation, and neurological or psychiatric disorders.

Gut testing, such as comprehensive stool analysis or intestinal permeability testing, may uncover imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, or increased gut permeability (leaky gut), which are common features of conditions like IBS, IBD, SIBO, and other gastrointestinal and neurological disorders.
Urine testing may assess levels of specific metabolites or neurotransmitters, providing additional insights into gut health, neurotransmitter balance, and systemic inflammation.

SWISS DETOX DIET / COLORADO CLEANSE

Both the Swiss Detox Diet, developed by Dr. Thomas Rau, and the Colorado Cleanse, developed by Dr. John Douillard, are comprehensive approaches to healing and detoxifying the gut, liver, and gallbladder.
Both programs are simple and consist of foods such as kitchari, olive oil, and celery juice.

If you need a liver or gallbladder cleanse, these protocols work well, and they can also be used as one-to-two-week jump-starts for any of the other diets in the beginner, intermediate, and advanced sections.
They’re good choices if you have any of the indicators of liver or gallbladder issues listed in the table.

The best books to read to better understand the protocols and get more recipes are Dr. Thomas Rau’sThe Swiss Secret to Optimal Healthand Dr. John Douillard’sColorado Cleanse, Eat Wheat, and Body, Mind, and Sport.
I am a fan of using either of these protocols as a cleanse once or twice a year, especially when I am not traveling and can give my body a little extra rest and recovery.
I also highly recommend a visit to the Swiss Mountain Clinic in the Swiss Alps for a done-for-you retreat that incorporates the Swiss Detox Diet.

I’ve been to this facility for a complete colon and liver detox, which combines European biological medicine practices with a detox diet for treatment of excessive toxins and also Lyme, Parkinson’s, mold and mycotoxin overload, cancer, and beyond.

You may want to follow this diet as a brief one-to-two-week cleanse if you have abnormal liver enzymes or poor gallbladder function as indicated by a blood test, high levels of toxins or metals, gastrointestinal discomfort, and/or difficulty with bowel movements and generally want a done-for- You short-term cleansing approach particularly relevant to liver and gallbladder function.

For example, low or high levels of alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, or gamma-glutamyl transferase can all be measured on a blood panel to assess liver and gallbladder health, while abnormal levels of bilirubin, urobilinogen, amylase, and lipase can be measured in the urine.
Yellow, tar-colored, or pale stool—along with higher levels of proteobacteria thanFirmicutes(types of gut bacteria that can indicate nonalcoholic fatty liver disease)—can also indicate issues.

CARNIVORE DIET
In chapter 14, I described my approach to and experience with the carnivore diet.

The diet originated in the early 1900s with an Arctic explorer named Vilhjalmur Stefansson, who noticed a near-complete absence of chronic diseases in the Inuit culture, where the diet consisted entirely of meats and animal fats.
He subsequently began experimenting with an all-meat diet, consuming nothing but meat and water for a year, and experienced noticeable results in his overall health and vitality.
The carnivore diet is a meat-based diet that excludes all sources of carbohydrates.
It is restrictive, allowing only proteins (beef, chicken, pork, and somefish), animal fats (primarily from the above meat sources), and Organ meats (such as liver, kidney, and bone marrow).
Other animal foods like dairy and eggs can also be consumed, and eating all animal parts such as organs, cartilage, and bones is encouraged.
Off-limits foods include nuts and seeds, legumes, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and all other plant- based foods.

While there are no clinical trials that assess the benefits of an all-meat diet, a 2021 survey involving over 2,000 participants who had been on a carnivore diet for at least six months showed self-reported improvements in sleep disruption, fatigue, brain fog, cognition, and mental clarity, being overweight or underweight, blood sugar dysregulation (type 1 and 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome), autoimmunity, joint and muscle pain, mental health, skin issues, and urinary difficulties.

I typically only recommend the carnivore diet as a short-term stint to heal the gut, which can happen when you eliminate all plant defense compounds and simplify the confusion offiguring out what’s aggravating you by eliminating just about everything—except meat.
Despite the fact that modern humans are omnivores, proponents of the carnivore meal plan believe that it is completely safe to stay on long term.

However, if you choose to do so, you must incorporate organ meats into your diet to avoid becoming deficient in certain nutrients, like B vitamins and vitamin C. Many folks who transition to this diet begin with a modified approach of intermittent fasting and including foods like honey, berries, squash, and cucumber (which is low in lectins and oxalates).

If you still experience symptoms on the carnivore diet, it could be a reaction to eggs, lactose, or fish, which you can also eliminate, but if you do, you need to include an iodine source, like iodized salt.

Finally, the carnivore diet is ketogenic, and you may experience keto adaptation (“ketoflu”) during thefirst two to four weeks, which can cause side effects like gas, bloating, abdominal pain, and loose stool due to the natural shift in the gut microbiome that occurs when switching to a low- Carb diet.
In this case, supplementing with electrolyte powders or drinks that contain sodium, potassium, and magnesium can help.
People who might benefit from a carnivore diet often report chronic digestive issues, autoimmune conditions, or inflammatory diseases that have not responded well to other dietary interventions.
Symptoms such as bloating, gas, joint pain, skin issues, and fatigue that persist despite trying other diets might suggest that this more “radical” dietary change could be beneficial.

Blood tests that might indicate a carnivore diet could be a goodfit include high levels of inflammation markers (such as C-reactive protein), unresolved deficiencies in B and iron (despite supplementation), 12autoimmune or food allergy issues (particularly sensitivities to grains, grasses, legumes, etc.), and lipid profiles that suggest an intolerance to carbohydrates (for example, elevated triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol).
Additionally, insulin resistance markers like fasting glucose and HbA1c levels might guide a recommendation to make this shift.
Genetic testing can provide insight into how well someone might tolerate a carnivore diet.

For instance, individuals with genetic predispositions to undermethylation may do better on a lower-plant, higher-meat diet, as would individuals who have an ancestral history of higher amounts of meat andfish rather than vegetables and fruits.
People who clear large amounts of LDL particles due to favorable PCSK9 genes may do better on a carnivore diet.

SIBO BI-PHASIC DIET (B-PD)
SIBO stands for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and it is characterized by the excessive growth of bacteria in the small intestine.
This condition can result from various factors, including maldigestion, malabsorption, and a leaky gut.
It can cause digestive and extraintestinal symptoms such as bloating, gas, abdominal pain, heartburn, constipation, diarrhea, rashes, headaches, and fatigue.

The SIBO Bi-Phasic Diet (SIBO B-PD) was developed by Dr. Nirala Jacobi to manage and treat SIBO, and it is one of the best systematic dietary approaches to eliminating gas and bloating when something like the SCD or basic low-FODMAP diet doesn’t seem to be working.
It combines principles of the low-FODMAP and SCD diets and is divided into two phases.

Thefirst phase restricts dietary fermentable carbohydrates (high-FODMAP foods like certain fruits, vegetables, grains, legumes, dairy products, sweeteners, and food additives) to reduce bacterial overgrowth and their production of metabolic by-products, relieve SIBO symptoms, heal the gut, and restore optimal digestive function.
The second phase introduces antimicrobial agents to remove any remaining bacterial overgrowth while reintroducing foods into the diet.
This phase also helps you identify trigger foods and maintain a healthy and balanced diet that supports gut health and prevents the recurrence of SIBO in the long term.
Phase 1 of the SIBO B-PD lasts two to six weeks and involves avoiding or minimizing intake of foods high in fermentable carbohydrates that can ferment in the gut and exacerbate symptoms.
This restrictive phase of the Diet emphasizes eating smaller, more frequent meals with adequate protein and healthy fat sources. Choices during this phase include•
Protein:poultry, beef, lamb, pork,fish, eggs•

Nonstarchy vegetables:leafy greens, zucchini, bell peppers, cucumbers, carrots, eggplant, bok choy• Healthy fats:olive oil, coconut oil, avocado, moderate amounts of nuts and seeds• Fermented foods (as tolerated):cultured vegetables, sauerkraut, kimchi•
Fruits:lemon, lime, berries•
Beverages:water, herbal teas, black coffee
Phase 2, the reintroduction phase, lasts four to six weeks.
The objective here is to gradually reintroduce foods to expand the diet and identify individual dietary triggers.
Phase 2 naturally progresses into the final phase of the SIBO B-PD—the maintenance phase.
The overall goal of the SIBO B-PD protocol is to create a sustainable, nutritious, and individualized dietary plan based on your tolerance levels.
Basic symptoms suggestive of SIBO and a potential benefit of this B- PD diet include chronic bloating, abdominal pain or discomfort, gas, diarrhea, constipation, and nutrient malabsorption.

Blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation, such as elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) or erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), as well as deficiencies in certain vitamins or minerals due to malabsorption.
Genetic testing may uncover gene variations associated with impaired gut motility or immune function, predisposing you to SIBO.
Gut testing, such as breath testing for hydrogen and methane gases, can confirm the presence of SIBO by detecting abnormal levels of these gases produced by bacteria in the small intestine.
Urine testing may reveal elevated levels of certain metabolites associated With bacterial overgrowth or gut dysbiosis, further supporting the diagnosis of SIBO.
A comprehensive stool test can also assess gut health by measuring markers that signal inflammation, intestinal permeability, dysbiosis, intestinal infection, and maldigestion.

A SIBO breath test, or the use of an at-home Food Marble device for breath testing, can monitor your SIBO treatment progress and confirm SIBO eradication by tracking changes in hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulfide gas levels.

ELEMENTAL DIET

Should you need to pull out all the stops to manage gut inflammation, SIBO, candida, yeast, fungus, constipation, FODMAP sensitivities, or leaky gut, or if you simply want to push the reset button on what seems to be problematic digestion, you can spend one to four weeks on an elemental diet.
It’s a good choice if you have the indicators of SIBO or FODMAP sensitivities, but no other solution, including any other diet in this chapter, seems to be working.
Warning:This diet is highly restrictive and only appropriate for a quick one-week to one-month stint.
The elemental diet is the simplest and, admittedly, most boring of all the beginner diet options.
It involves consuming a meal replacement formula for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, along with a few extra oils, fats, and amino acids for added nutrients.
For a meal replacement drink, I recommend one or two servings of Thorne’s Mediclear SGS or Dr. Ruscio’s Elemental Health formula.

For extra protein, fat, and calories, you can blend the formula with bone broth and/or add 10 to 20 g essential amino acids to each shake, along with a teaspoon or tablespoon of extra-virgin olive oil and MCT or coconut oil.

These formulas are expensive, so you can also use my DIY version of an elemental health smoothie, which tastes like an orange creamsicle (though you may still tire of orange creamsicles after a month!).

Blend the following: ice and organic coconut water to the desired texture, a liquid multivitamin (Mary Ruth’s is good), 10 g essential amino acids (mango flavor Kion Aminos works well for this recipe), a dash of natural vanilla extract, a pinch of salt, a tablespoon of honey, and an ounce of extra-virgin olive oil.
I’ll include a video of me making it on the resources page for this chapter.
Should you want even more variety, you can include soups, broths, and steamed vegetables in your evening meal.
To learn more about the elemental diet and what can and cannot be included, I recommend Dr. Allison Siebecker’s website, SIBOInfo.com.

In this section, I’ll introduce you to my favorite diets that are clean and easy to digest and consist primarily of real, whole foods.
Many of the diets in this section tend to be low-carbohydrate or ketogenic.
This is not because a ketogenic diet is perfect for everyone but because eating carbohydrates throughout the day can lead to blood sugar fluctuations and inflammation.

A low-carbohydrate or ketogenic approach is a good way to avoid this, and most people have the most stable energy levels when they consume no more than around 30 percent of their calories from carbohydrates, especially starches and sugars.

For athletes, extremely active individuals, folks with the AMY1 gene variant (which allows them to consume more carbohydrates), and people who need more carbohydrates, I do recommend prioritizing the addition of extra nightly carbohydrates to the diets in this section.

In this type of “refeed” scenario, you can add 50 to 250 g (depending on your size and activity level) of clean starches in the form of sweet potatoes, yams, taro, other tubers, parsnips, carrots, beets, rice, or properly prepared (either soaked, sprouted, or fermented) grains, with foods such as dark chocolate, berries, or coconut or organic dairy ice cream for dessert.
Highly active individuals may also benefit from a weekly carbohydrate refeed scenario, a day on which carbs make up about 40 percent of your daily caloric intake.
WAHLS PROTOCOL (LOW-CARB VERSION)
After being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), Dr. Terry Wahls began studying food and vitamins and created a nutrient-rich, Paleo-esque diet.
Within a year of changing her way of eating, she was out of her wheelchair and biking miles at a time.
The best book to read to learn more about this plan is her bookThe Wahls Protocol.

On the Wahls Protocol, you eat lots of meat andfish, vegetables (especially green, leafy ones), brightly colored fruit like berries, and fat from animal and plant sources (especially omega-3 fatty acids), and you avoid dairy, eggs, grain, legumes, nightshades, and sugar.

The low-carb version of the Wahls Protocol is especially good for managing autoimmune conditions while introducing a bit more variety than the AIP. This diet can also work well for those with mast cell issues aggravated by mold and mycotoxins or Lyme, and for those with mitochondrial dysfunction or poor nervous system health.

Symptoms of conditions that may benefit from the Wahls Protocol include chronic fatigue, muscle weakness, cognitive difficulties, mood disturbances, and neurological symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or balance problems.

From a testing standpoint, blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation or immune dysregulation, such as elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines, autoimmune antibodies, or markers of oxidative stress, which are commonly associated with autoimmune conditions, neurological disorders, and chronic inflammatory conditions.
Genetic testing may identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurological or autoimmune disorders.

Gut testing, such as comprehensive stool analysis or microbial profiling, may uncover imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, or increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are common features of conditions like IBD, IBS, SIBO, and other gastrointestinal and autoimmune disorders.
Urine testing can also show increased levels of Specific metabolites related to inflammatory markers that suggest impairments in mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation.
Based on assessments like this, if you have confirmed or suspected autoimmune, neurological, or chronic inflammatory conditions, you may benefit from following the Wahls Protocol.

PLANT PARADOX DIET

The Plant Paradox diet, developed by Dr. Stephen Gundry and described in his bookThe Plant Paradox, eliminates lectins (a natural plant-based defensive protein that can cause gastric distress in many people and is found in foods such as green beans, lentils, and edamame) and limits sugar and polyunsaturated omega-6 fats.

It also limits phytates, which are a source of energy for sprouting seeds; when people eat them in plants (as phytic acid), they bind to nutrients like manganese, iron, and zinc, making them indigestible and increasing your risk of being deficient in those minerals.

The Plant Paradox diet usually starts with a three-day cleanse, during which you repopulate your gut bacteria with leafy greens, cruciferous vegetables, clean protein, and good fats, and then has a second phase in which you eat only from the list of approved foods for at least six weeks.
On the resources page for this chapter, I’ve simplified the diet to skip the Two phases and still give you a lectin-free protocol; this version also uses a ketogenic strategy to control blood sugar.

I recommend this diet if you want to eat a rich variety of vegetables but have difficulty digesting them and are sensitive to lectins, phytates, oxalates, and other built-in plant defense mechanisms—it lets you consume a diverse array of plants prepared in a manner that makes them easier to digest.
It’s a good choice if you have indicators of plant-, legume-, or grain-digesting issues, such as gluten sensitivities, IBS, or other problematic responses to nuts, seeds, and legumes.

Many mineral deficiency symptoms can occur due to phytates, including paleness, dizziness, dry hair and skin, restless legs, anxiety, headaches, and fatigue (iron deficiency); diarrhea, hair loss, poor immune function, and loss of appetite (zinc deficiency); or low fertility and impaired glucose tolerance (manganese deficiency).

You may also have markers of inflammation or autoimmune issues such as low levels of blood TNF-alpha, adiponectin, or interleukin-6; a low white blood cell count; low ferritin; or low T3. These, along with a food allergy and intolerance test (see chapter 16), can give you insight into whether modulating plant intake may be a good idea for you.

PALEO DIET

The Paleo diet isflexible and can be adapted for your specific needs, but it essentially cuts out modern agricultural foods that can cause an inflammatory reaction in many people and focuses on foods that our Paleolithic ancestors would likely have eaten, depending on seasonal availability.
One of the fundamental concepts behind Paleo is that humans were hunter-gatherers far longer than they’ve been farmers and cultivators.
As a result, our genes evolved to favor the nutrient-dense plants and meats of those hunter-gatherers, not the high-sugar, high-dairy, high-refined-carb modern Western diet.

The standard Paleo diet includes meat (especially organ meats like liver and kidneys, bone broth, and marrow); high-quality animal fats; seafood; eggs (ideally, pasture-raised); nonstarchy vegetables; low- glycemic-index fruits like berries, citrus, and stone fruits; coconut oil, olive oil, and avocado oil; nuts and seeds; and herbs and spices.

The inflammatory foods excluded from the Paleo diet include grains like wheat, barley, oats, corn, and rice; dairy; refined sugar; processed foods; and vegetable oils (such as soybean, peanut, corn, and canola oils).
Foods that are eaten in moderate amounts (if they are well-tolerated) include legumes like lentils and chickpeas and nightshades such as tomatoes, white potatoes, red potatoes, and peppers.

In other words, eat like a human being would have eaten prior to the agricultural revolution— perhaps with the exception of all the modern, newfangled “Paleo- approved” energy bars, drinks, and supplements that have saturated the market!
The best guide to more history and details of the Paleo diet isThe Paleo Solutionby Robb Wolf.

The Paleo diet would be appropriate for someone sensitive to grains, legumes, and dairy who wants to expand their eating beyond a more restrictive protocol such as Autoimmune Paleo (AIP), and it may be helpful for conditions of gut inflammation, autoimmune disease, or skin Issues such as acne or eczema.
Some research even suggests that type 2 diabetes may improve with a Paleo diet.
This is because insulin resistance may be caused by inflammation, and the Paleo diet eliminates common inflammatory foods.
It’s a good choice if you have any indicators of dairy sensitivities, autoimmune disorders, or gut inflammation.

A note on dairy: You can consume dairy on a Paleo diet if you tolerate it well and it comes from grass-fed cows, which produce milk that is higher in anti-inflammatory omega-3 fatty acids and lower in inflammatory omega-6s.
Grain-fed cows absorb gut-irritating lectins from their feed that are then concentrated in their milk, which can contribute to inflammation in people who drink that milk.

Ideally, any milk consumed on a Paleo diet (or, in my opinion, any other diet) should be A2 milk, which has more A2 than A1 casein—A1 casein can produce significant gut inflammation in many individuals.
Casein concentrations vary among breeds of cows, with some breeds—such as Guernsey and Jersey cows—having very little to no A1 casein. You canfind more details at A2Milk.com.

MEDITERRANEAN DIET (LOW-CARB VERSION)

The Mediterranean diet is a plant- and omega-3-rich diet that is prevalent in many longevity hot spots and Blue Zones (although it is possible that the diet’s positive health effects may also be caused by lifestyle factors such as fasting, seasonal eating, social meals, high intake of tannin-rich beverages and wild plants, and limited meat consumption).

It is a dietary pattern inspired by the traditional eating habits of countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea and emphasizes whole, minimally processed foods such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, olive oil,fish, and poultry while limiting intake of processed red meat, refined sugars, and unhealthy fats.
The diet is rich infiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and phytonutrients, which have been shown to reduce inflammation, improve blood lipid levels, lower blood pressure, and support heart health.

A low-carb twist on the Mediterranean diet merges the well-known beneficial health impacts of the Mediterranean diet with the positive metabolic effects of stable blood sugar, elevated ketones, fat-burning metabolism, and low intake of processed starches and carbohydrates.

After all, a traditional, healthy Mediterranean meal doesn’t include unlimited breadsticks and endless salad bowls drenched in vegetable oil, and instead incorporates a much wider variety of plants, herbs, spices, Fattyfish, avocados, olive oil, fermented dairy, artisanal cheeses, and more in a rainbow of colors.

Based on a large amount of epidemiological research, this approach can be particularly effective for managing cardiovascular conditions, improving heart health, and managing metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, along with overall health span and lifespan.

ANCESTRAL DIET

There are a variety of ways to customize the Weston A. Price diet to your specific ancestry—a concept explored in chapter 19. In the bookThe Jungle Effect, Dr. Daphne Miller explains the dietary wisdom of traditional cultures whose diets are specific to their genes and ancestry.

In her research for the book (you can listen to my podcast with her, linked to on BoundlessBook.com/21), Miller traveled to locations around the world that she identified as “cold spots”—the opposite of hot spots!—that had a remarkably low incidence of diseases such as diabetes, heart disease, depression, colon cancer, breast cancer, and prostate cancer.
It turned out that many of the traditional cultures in these areas ate whole-food, Weston A. Price–like diets that were specific to their traditions, ancestry, and local environment.
Many cold-spot inhabitants who relocate and switch to a modern Western diet develop the very diseases for which their traditional environments are cold spots!

The following are examples of cold spots and foods frequently eaten in their ancestral diets:• Copper Canyon, Mexico (diabetes cold spot):corn, beans, squash, peppers, nopal cactus, onions, cilantro, tomatoes, jicama, nuts, Avocados• Crete (heart disease cold spot):olive oil, chickpeas, lentils, whole- grain pasta, potatoes, Swiss chard, kale, arugula,fish, red wine,figs, walnuts• Iceland (depression cold spot):fish, walnuts, purslane,flaxseed oil, barley, rye, black tea, beans, split peas, potatoes, organic dairy products, omega-3-enriched eggs, wild game, cabbage, bilberries• Cameroon, West Africa (colon cancer cold spot):millet, teff, collard greens, mustard greens, spinach, okra, plantains, beans, nuts,fish, wild poultry and game, onions, tomatoes, bananas, yogurt, kefir, fermented vegetables• Okinawa, Japan (breast and prostate cancers cold spot):tofu, tempeh, miso,fish, cabbage, bok choy, broccoli, kale, cauliflower, brown rice, green tea, sea vegetables, sweet potatoes, mushrooms, tomatoes, watermelons, grapefruit For more information, read Dr. Miller’s book.
Two other very good titles on ancestral eating are Dr. Michael Smith’sReturning to an Ancestral Dietand Stephen Le’s100 Million Years of Food.

Follow this eating plan if you’ve done DNA testing and/or know your genetics and family history, and you want to try eating more like your ancestors, which for many can be ideal for health, cognition, performance, fertility, and longevity.

THE BOUNDLESS SUPPLEMENT
PROGRAM

In an ideal world, you would be able to fully customize every supplement you take to your unique physiology—especially based on the information in chapter 16—rather than follow a cookie-cutter program.
But I’ve included suggestions for supplementation protocols that paint with a relatively broad brush and cover most bases for beginner, intermediate, and advanced goals.

Beginner This protocol is for you if you are on a budget, want the lowest-hanging fruit to give you 80 percent of the results with 20 percent of the expense and effort, or need the minimum effective dose of supplementation to look, feel, and perform as good as possible each day.
Include the following: • A multivitamin-multimineral complex, such as the Thorne Multi capsules or MaryRuth’s liquid

• A goodfish oil, such as Kion Omega—1–2 g per day with a meal • Creatine—5 g per day, taken with a meal or smoothie or another beverage, split into two 2.5 g servings (one in the morning, one in the evening).
The brand is not important as long as there are no added sweeteners orfillers, and basic creatine monohydrate isfine. Kion Creatine is my recommended option.

• If you are traveling or unable to eat a wide range of plants, an organic greens powder such as AG1 Greens, OrganifiGreens, or PaleoValley • If you have difficulty sleeping, a sleep stack of magnesium, CBD, a relaxing cocktail like Kion Sleep or any adaptogenic herbal blend, and, if traveling, melatonin

• If you have gut issues or are unable to eat a wide variety of fermented foods, a good probiotic and digestive enzyme blend, such as Seed Probiotic or Thorne Advanced Digestive Enzymes Intermediate This protocol is for you if you have a slightly higher budget and want to add supplements that can further enhance performance, longevity, and mental function without breaking the bank.
Follow the beginner protocol and add the following: • 10–20 g of essential amino acids (EAAs) per day—preferably pre- or • Exogenous ketones for fasted or longer workouts or busy days

• Prior to your largest meal or largest carb-containing meal of the day, insulin-stabilizing foods or supplements like bitter melon extract (Kion Lean is good), Ceylon cinnamon, apple cider vinegar, berberine, rosemary, turmeric, ginger, fenugreek,Gymnema sylvestre, or cayenne • On more cognitively demanding days, coffee or green tea blended with adaptogenic compounds such as L-theanine, tulsi, reishi or astragalus, or small amounts of nicotine Advanced This protocol is for you if you are willing to invest in better living through science so you can live as long as possible and perform at a high level, and you desire to incorporate a full-blown Boundless supplement protocol.

Follow the intermediate protocol and add the following: • Qualia, Nootopia, TianChi, Wukiyo, microdosing, or any other nootropic stack or adaptogenic herb blend, especially on more cognitively demanding days (see chapter 5)

• Hydrogen-rich water (dissolve tablets in water, use a hydrogen bottle, purchase canned hydrogen-rich water, or use a hydrogen water– generating machine) • Daily supplementation with a good longevity stack, including some of the most important recommendations from chapter 19, such as spermidine, urolithin-A, astaxanthin, curcumin, CoQ10, PQQ, glutathione or NAC, pterostilbene, MitoQ, astragalus, C60, nicotinamide riboside (NR), and peptides Obviously, you may have specific needs for other supplements.
